title: Tool approval and limits
description: Which actions an agent takes on its own and which only with your “OK”: risk classes, per-call assessment, the default rule and hooks.

steps.question: You want an agent that reads your calendar silently but freezes and waits for your “OK” before sending an email. Where do you start?
steps.answer: You don't have to set anything up: that's how the app works by default. The agent reads and writes on its own, but sends anything outside or deletes only with your “OK.” Agent hooks are for when you want it to ask about something else too, for example before setting an alarm.

steps.text: In the lesson on tools the agent got hands: look at the calendar, set a reminder, open an email draft. But hands come in different strengths. Giving an agent the same access to “read” and to “delete forever” is dangerous. That's why every call has a risk label.

steps.imagePrompt: A small robot walks along a hallway of three doors with traffic lights: green over a door with a reading lamp, yellow over a door with a pencil, red over a door with an envelope flying out, where the robot waits for a human thumbs up.
steps.caption: The riskier the action, the stricter the consent

steps.definition: A label for how dangerous an action is, from harmless reading to irreversible deletion. It's a way of thinking: it helps decide where the agent can act silently and where a person is needed.
steps.example: “Read the calendar” is safe, so let it happen silently. “Delete a file” can't be undone, so it makes sense to ask first.

steps.text: There are four classes. “Read only” looks and changes nothing. “Changes data” writes or edits something on the device. “Leaves the device” sends data outside, onto the network. “Can delete irreversibly” is the most dangerous: there's no rolling it back.

steps.instruction: Match each risk class to what it means:

pairs.def: Sends data outside, onto the network
An action you can't roll back

steps.text: The default rule in this app: “read only” and “changes data” the agent does on its own. “Leaves the device” and “can delete irreversibly” happen only with your “OK.” In the background, when there is nobody to answer, such calls are simply forbidden. Agent hooks can add to this: require an “OK” for a specific tool, or forbid it altogether. And when you build your own agent and tick a risky tool on the review screen, the app asks “Turn on?” once and explains the consequences.

steps.situation: The “Reminders” tool has a peaceful action: show the list. And it also has “cancel a reminder.”
steps.q: What risk class does the “cancel” call have?
options: “Can delete irreversibly”: risk is judged per call, not per tool
“Read only”: the tool mostly reads, so this call does too
None: canceling reminders counts as a completely safe action
steps.explain: Risk is judged for each call, not for the tool as a whole. One dangerous action inside a peaceful tool raises the bar for that call only. You can see it from the icon on the confirmation bar. And such a call asks for your “OK” even without hooks.

steps.text: What it looks like. When a call is risky, like sending something outside or deleting, or an agent hook requires confirmation, the turn freezes before the call. A bar appears at the bottom of the chat: “The agent needs permission.” It shows which tool, the risk icon for this particular call, the arguments, and two buttons: “Allow” or “Deny.” Until you decide, the agent waits and does nothing.

steps.caption: The default rule: read and write silently, send and delete with your “OK.” Tap “Next call” and decide for yourself

steps.text: Practice. After the lesson, ask me in an ordinary chat: “write Anna an email saying I'll be late.” Email leaves the device, so the bar “The agent needs permission” appears at the bottom of the chat. Without your “OK,” the draft won't open. Tap “Deny” and see what I say. But “set an alarm for 7:00” will go through without a question, because it's a write.

In short. A risk class is a way to think about how dangerous an action is: read only, change, send outside, irreversible deletion. It is judged for each call, not for the tool as a whole. By default, reading and writing go on their own, while sending outside and deleting wait for your “OK” on the confirmation bar, and in the background they are forbidden. Hooks can add a confirmation or a ban for a specific tool.

questions.q: Which calls ask for your “OK” even without hooks?
options: None: without hooks everything runs silently
questions.explain: That is the default rule: “leaves the device” and “can delete irreversibly” wait for your decision. Reading and writing go on their own, unless a hook says otherwise.

questions.q: A tool is peaceful, but it has an irreversible action. What risk does that call have?
options: Irreversible: risk is judged by the specific action, not by the tool
Read only: the class is set for the whole tool and doesn't change with the action
None, until you turn on a special strict mode in the settings
questions.explain: Risk is assessed for each call. A dangerous action raises the bar for itself.

questions.q: What happens while the agent waits for your decision on the confirmation bar?
options: The turn freezes: the agent does nothing until you choose “Allow” or “Deny”
The agent does the action right away, and you can undo it a bit later if you want
The whole turn stops with an error and you have to start the task again
questions.explain: Until you confirm, the agent stays paused and doesn't touch the risky action.

questions.q: The agent wakes up at night on a schedule and wants to delete a calendar event. What happens?
options: The call is forbidden: nobody is there to confirm it
It deletes it and sends a report in the morning
It waits until morning and asks you
questions.explain: There is no screen in the background, and nobody to give an “OK.” So sending outside and deleting are simply forbidden there.
